Problem[edit]

Emily has a red sheet of paper. She draws 2026 circles (not necessarily of equal size) on the piece of paper. She chooses a circle to color black, then cuts the paper around the circumference of all 2026 circles. She then separates the pieces of paper, into at least 2 black pieces and some number of red pieces. Is it possible that all black pieces are congruent?

Solution[edit]

Consider convexity. A circle is convex all throughout the perimeter, so any cut it makes is convex for half of the cut (the part closer to the circle's center) and is concave for the other part. So the main claim is that there always exists a purely convex black part as well as a part with both concave and convex sides. The prior can be proved by induction.

We start off with a single circle which is convex. Take that as the base case. Now assume by induction we have a piece that is completely convex. A extra cut through that piece can separate it into 2 pieces, a piece with a hole through it or 3 pieces. If it is 2 pieces, it is easy to see that the piece closer to the center has a convex side added, which means the shape is purely convex. If there is a piece with a hole, the "hole" itself as a circle is purely convex. If 3 pieces are created, the middle piece has 2 extra convex sides, which maintains the purely-convexity. So by induction there exists a piece that is purely convex.

Next we can prove that there also exists a concave shape. There are at least 2 black pieces, so there must be at least one cut of a circle through a circle which creates at least one concave piece. Then, no number of convex cuts can make the concave arc "no longer concave". So the concave arc always exists, meaning there is always a concave shape.

A concave shape is definitely not congruent to a convex shape, so it is impossible for all pieces to be congruent.

~WYC10041

Solution 2 (Concordance, Another version of Convexity)[edit]

No, it is not possible.

The extrema case is when two pieces are formed. Showing that the minima does not work proves that no matter how the minima increases there will always be a way to evaluate the diagram like the minima, and thus no cases will be prevalent.

:

It must be the case that a Black and Red circle overlap.

:

There must exist two black pieces. Consider overlapping the red and black circles. Then, cutting the circumference of the red circle yields a black piece. Cutting the circumference of what remains of the black and red circle overlap yields another black piece. If the circles are disjoint, then there would only exist red pieces, contradicting the problem statement, hence proven.

There will exist at least one black piece that is never congruent to all following black pieces.

Through Lemma 1 the circles must overlap.

The case never holds if two circles, one red and one black, lie on the plane overlapping. Then, if the number of circles increase to 2026, I can always choose a red circle and a black circle, and two red circles with a bounded black union, and through the direct result of Lemma 2 imply that no such configuration exists.

Therefore, no matter how we arrange the circles on the plane, it will never be possible.
